newsitem.title: USA: NY Gov hired bond lawyers who gave money-Leichter.
newsitem.headline: NY Gov hired bond lawyers who gave money-Leichter.

text.p: A New York State Senator who has attacked Gov. George Pataki on campaign contributions and jobs growth, said Tuesday big contributions made by bond law firms helped them win lucrative contracts from the state.

Franz Leichter, a Manhattan Democrat, released a report he said showed the Republican governor gave work on municipal bonds to 14 law firms that contributed to committees controlled by Pataki and the state Republican party.

"It appears that the Pataki Administration has completely politicized the awarding of municipal bond business," the state senator said, in prepared remarks. "Law firms that make political contributions to Pataki and the state GOP appear to have a much greater chance of being selected as bond counsel on municipal bond issues in New York."

Leichter's report singled out Haythe & Curley, whose partners include Charles Dorkey, which he said the Albany Times Union listed as one of Pataki's 10 biggest donors, Rogers & Wells, whose roster includes L. Bart Stone, the treasurer of the Republican state committee, and Fischbein, Badillo, Wagner & Harding, which has Raymond Harding, who leads the Liberal Party, as a partner.
The law firms and spokesmen for Pataki and D'Amato were not immediately available to comment.

The report said that municipal bond lawyers from 1994 to July 1997 gave nearly four times more to committees controlled by Pataki, U.S. Senator Alfonse D'Amato, and the state GOP, than to Democrats, including state Comptroller H. Carl McCall, and other state Democratic committees.
State Republicans received $415,508 from the bond law firms and lawyers, while Democrats got $116,491.
Leichter said the vast majority of governmental bonds issued in New York are sold by public authorities, which are all run by Pataki appointees.

While former Gov. Mario Cuomo between 1992 and 1994 also got political contributions from law firms, the state senator said the practice escalated sharply under Pataki, an upswing that he attributed to ban on such gifts from municipal underwriters, called G-37, which began in 1994.

The former Democrat governor got $54,250 from law firms that served as bond counsel, while other state Democrat committees took in $63,725, he said. However, Cuomo got no political contributions from bond lawyers in 1992 to 1993.
